teaser: An emperor bought it on sight. A young novelist said she was made of marzipan.
review_notes:
Napoleon III bought the painting for his personal collection at the 1863 Salon (standard account; no price given in the lesson).
Salon of 1863: jury rejections (about 3,000 works, often given as more than half of submissions) leading to the Salon des Refusés, where Manet showed Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe.
Cabanel elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 1863 and appointed professor at the École des Beaux-Arts shortly after (1863/1864).
Zola's remark, given as a paraphrase: Venus 'drowned in a river of milk', like a courtesan made 'of a sort of pink and white marzipan' (written in 1867). Check before quoting directly.
Her eyes: the lesson says her eyelids are not quite closed and she seems to look out from under her arm. This is the usual reading, but in our small image the eye looks nearly shut. A human should confirm on the zoom image that the find spot (0.755, 0.58) shows it well enough.
Smaller replica painted in 1875 for the American collector John Wolfe, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Dimensions 130 x 225 cm.

lesson.text: In the spring of 1863, one visitor to the big Paris art show liked this painting so much that he bought it for himself. The visitor was Napoleon III, emperor of the French. It is hard to imagine a better customer, or a clearer sign of what official France wanted from art.

The show was the Salon, the yearly exhibition where a jury decided which artists the public would see. That same year the jury turned away about three thousand works. The protests were so loud that the emperor allowed a separate show for the rejected. One of them was a picture by Édouard Manet with a naked woman at a picnic, and the crowds came to laugh at it.
Same year, same city, two nudes: one bought by the emperor, one mocked by the crowd. The difference between them explains what “academic art” means.

Academic art is art made by the rules of the official schools: a noble subject taken from myth or history, perfect drawing, and a surface so smooth that no brush mark shows. Alexandre Cabanel was its star. Here the noble subject is Venus, Roman goddess of love, who according to the myth was born fully grown from the foam of the sea.

The myth was the alibi. A naked Parisian woman would have been indecent. A naked goddess was culture. Five putti, the chubby winged babies of old paintings, fly overhead and blow seashell trumpets to announce her. Still, something in her face is not quite as innocent as a newborn's.
Venus seems asleep, one arm thrown over her forehead. Is she? Tap the spot that makes you doubt it.

spots.title: Not quite asleep
spots.text: In the shadow of her arm, her eyelids are not fully shut. She seems to glance out at whoever is looking. The pose says “sleeping goddess”, the eyes say she knows you are there.

lesson.text: That small detail did not escape people at the time. The young writer Émile Zola, a friend of Manet, mocked this Venus as a pretty courtesan drowned in a river of milk, made not of flesh but of pink and white marzipan. He meant the paint itself: too sweet, too soft, too perfect to be a body.

The year 1863 was very good to Cabanel. Besides the emperor's purchase, he was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts, the small club of artists that ruled French art, and became a professor at its famous school in Paris. For the next twenty-five years he trained hundreds of students and sat on the Salon jury.

Zola was unfair about one thing: this kind of surface is extremely hard to produce. Painters called it the “licked” finish. It took thin layers of oil paint, blended while wet with soft brushes until every transition disappeared. Compare three areas of the canvas to see where Cabanel hides his hand, and where he lets it show.

lesson.title: Three kinds of paint
lesson.text: The canvas is 130 by 225 cm (about 4 by 7.5 feet), and Venus is close to life-size. See how the paint changes from one zone to the next.

spots.title: Skin like porcelain
spots.text: No vein, no crease, no body hair, no visible stroke. Light slides from hip to shoulder in one unbroken gradation. This is the marzipan Zola made fun of.

spots.title: Foam
spots.text: Here the brush is allowed to show. Thicker white dabs make the froth she was born from, and her red-gold hair floats on it and trails out over the water.

spots.title: The herald
spots.text: A putto blows into a seashell, wings out, cheeks puffed. His body dissolves a little into the pale sky, which keeps your attention on the goddess below.

lesson.text: After the smooth body, the sea feels almost rough. Cabanel knew what he was doing: a little texture around the figure makes her skin look even more polished. It is also why she seems to float on the wave more than lie in it. Nothing wet touches her.

The picture was so popular that Cabanel painted it again. In 1875 an American collector, John Wolfe, ordered a smaller version, and it now hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Repeating a hit for a paying client was normal business for a successful Salon painter.

Then taste turned over. Manet and the Impressionists, laughed at in the 1860s, became the heroes of modern art, and painters like Cabanel were pushed into storage for most of the twentieth century. Today this Venus hangs in the Musée d'Orsay, a short walk from Manet's rejected picnic. Which one would you have bought in 1863? Be honest.

quiz.question: Who bought the painting at the 1863 Salon?
quiz.explanation: The emperor bought it for his own collection.

quiz.question: What is the “licked” finish?
options: Thick paint applied with a knife
A surface so blended that no brush mark shows
quiz.explanation: Thin layers were blended while wet until every transition disappeared.

quiz.question: According to the myth, how was Venus born?
options: From the foam of the sea
quiz.explanation: She was born fully grown from sea foam, which Cabanel paints under her.

quiz.question: What did Zola compare this Venus to?
quiz.explanation: He found the painted flesh too sweet and soft to be a real body.

facts.text: Cabanel was rejected by the Salon jury in 1863.
facts.explanation: He triumphed there. The rejected artists, like Manet, were shown separately.

facts.text: A second, smaller version of the painting is in New York.
facts.explanation: Cabanel painted it in 1875 for the collector John Wolfe.

facts.text: The winged babies in the sky are called putti.
facts.explanation: Putti are the chubby winged infants of older European painting.
